action_criteria.expected_evidence: MoCA 21/30 with visuospatial losses (cube, clock, floor plan) and delayed recall 1/5 not rescued by cueing (3/5 multiple choice), attention and fluency largely spared; informant FAQ 14/30
action_criteria.label: Perform a validated bedside cognitive assessment and record the per-domain profile and whether delayed recall improves with cueing
action_criteria.rationale: A visuospatial-led decline in an architect needs a documented profile, including whether recall responds to cues, before the white matter burden is credited with it.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Visuospatial and constructional performance at the 1st-3rd percentile and recognition at the 8th, with processing speed and fluency within normal limits
action_criteria.label: Order formal multi-domain neuropsychological testing to settle the executive-versus-amnestic attribution and to document a baseline for follow-up
action_criteria.rationale: Separate measures of visuospatial function, recognition memory and processing speed show which way the cognitive dissociation runs.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: All results within reference ranges, including TSH, B12, folate, RPR, HIV, HbA1c 5.6% and LDL 82 mg/dL on rosuvastatin
action_criteria.label: Order the reversible-cause screen and the vascular-risk assays that will be treated (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate, HbA1c, lipid panel)
action_criteria.rationale: The reversible-cause screen is part of every dementia work-up and the vascular risk values guide treatment of the small-vessel burden.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Fazekas 3 white matter hyperintensity with two lacunes alongside marked posterior cortical atrophy (Koedam 2-3) and Scheltens MTA grade 2; no microbleeds
action_criteria.label: Obtain brain MRI reported in STRIVE-2 terms (FLAIR with a Fazekas grade, T1/T2 for lacunes, DWI for chronicity, SWI for microbleeds and siderosis) with the medial temporal and posterior atrophy scores
action_criteria.rationale: The atrophy pattern has to be read alongside the white matter burden that prompted the referral.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Positive amyloid PET with posterior predominance, composite SUVr 1.61
action_criteria.label: Obtain amyloid PET to establish amyloid status, since he refuses lumbar puncture
action_criteria.rationale: A posterior cortical and amnestic syndrome beside a severe small-vessel burden is the mixed question; he refuses any spinal procedure, so amyloid PET is the route.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Marked posterior parietal, precuneus and posterior cingulate hypometabolism with only mild patchy frontal defects adjacent to the white matter lesions
action_criteria.label: Obtain FDG-PET to separate a temporoparietal Alzheimer pattern from the patchy multifocal hypometabolism that follows white matter lesions
action_criteria.rationale: FDG-PET shows whether the metabolic deficit follows the posterior cortex or the white matter lesions.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose vascular dementia from a Fazekas 3 burden when the cognitive dissociation points the other way.
Do not pursue a lumbar puncture in a patient who refuses spinal procedures when amyloid PET answers the same question.
Do not omit vascular risk-factor treatment because the leading pathology is degenerative.
Do not start an antiplatelet for covert small-vessel disease alone [ESO_2021_SVD].
Do not rely on the absence of informant concern to clear driving when visuospatial testing is at the 1st percentile.
Do not prescribe anticholinergic medications alongside a cholinesterase inhibitor.
required_recommendations: Name mixed dementia with a posterior-predominant Alzheimer syndrome (visuospatial-led, storage-type amnesia, posterior atrophy, positive amyloid PET) as the leading pathology and severe coexisting small-vessel disease [VASCOG_2014].
Offer a cholinesterase inhibitor for the Alzheimer component (e.g. donepezil 5 mg at night, 10 mg after 4-6 weeks if tolerated) [NICE_NG97].

Treat the small-vessel burden: lower blood pressure gradually to below 130/80 mmHg (144/84 on olmesartan and amlodipine), checking orthostatic blood pressure, continue rosuvastatin and CPAP [ESO_2021_SVD].
Arrange a formal driving assessment and advise him not to drive until it is done: visuospatial function is at the 1st-3rd percentile despite no informant concern.
Offer occupational therapy and visual strategies for the visuospatial deficit, carer support for his wife, advance care planning and review in 6-12 months [NICE_NG97].

avoided_actions.rationale: A gradual three-year decline without fluctuation or episodes: EEG answers no question in this patient.
Visuospatial failure without parkinsonism, fluctuation, hallucinations or dream enactment: a dopamine transporter scan answers no question in this patient.
No core feature of Lewy body disease; cardiac sympathetic imaging answers no question in this patient.
A gradual three-year decline is not the subacute multidomain syndrome that indicates paraneoplastic or autoimmune encephalitis antibodies.
MRI is available and not contraindicated; CT cannot show microbleeds, siderosis or small lacunes.
No clinical stroke and no cortical or territorial infarct: there is no embolic pattern for an echocardiogram to explain.
No clinical stroke, no cortical infarct and a regular pulse: prolonged rhythm monitoring would not change the diagnosis or the treatment.
Mr Ferri has declined lumbar puncture after a difficult lumbar fusion; amyloid PET answers the same question.

accepted: Mixed Alzheimer and vascular dementia, with a posterior-predominant Alzheimer syndrome as the leading pathology and severe coexisting small-vessel disease

differential.key_features: This is what the Fazekas 3 burden and the referral invite, but the cognitive dissociation runs the wrong way (visuospatial function at the 1st percentile, processing speed at the 26th) and amyloid PET is positive with posterior predominance

differential.diagnosis: Posterior cortical atrophy (Alzheimer disease) without significant vascular contribution
differential.key_features: The visuospatial-led syndrome with posterior atrophy and positive amyloid fits the Alzheimer component, but a Fazekas 3 burden with two lacunes is a genuine second contributor that needs its own treatment
Visuospatial failure is prominent in DLB, but there are no hallucinations, no fluctuation, no parkinsonism and no dream enactment
CPAP adherence is good and the profile is not the attentional pattern of untreated apnoea
No limb apraxia to command, no alien limb, no asymmetric rigidity or myoclonus

key_clinical_evidence: The direction of the cognitive dissociation identifies the pathology: subcortical vascular disease slows processing while sparing posterior cortical function, and this patient shows the reverse
A striking white matter burden is not evidence of the mechanism of a cognitive syndrome whose shape does not fit it: imaging severity and clinical relevance are different questions
The FDG pattern adds an independent argument: hypometabolism follows the posterior cortex rather than the extent of the white matter lesions
Amyloid PET substitutes for CSF where a patient refuses a lumbar puncture, and the refusal is a legitimate clinical constraint rather than an obstacle to be argued away
The vascular burden still requires treatment even when it is not the leading pathology, because it accelerates the degenerative decline

metadata.difficulty_rationale: Puzzle: the referral, the imaging and the risk factors all point to vascular dementia, and the diagnosis turns on the direction of the cognitive dissociation and on a biomarker obtained by an acceptable route
key_educational_points: The direction of a cognitive dissociation identifies the pathology more reliably than the severity of an imaging finding
Posterior cortical atrophy scores belong in the report of a dementia MRI alongside the white matter grade
FDG hypometabolism that does not follow the white matter lesions argues against a vascular mechanism
A refused lumbar puncture is a reason to use amyloid PET, not a reason to abandon biomarkers

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Claudio Ferri is a 70-year-old retired architect who was referred after an MRI performed for headache showed extensive white matter change. He and his wife describe three years of difficulty that began with drawing and spatial tasks: he could no longer sketch a floor plan to scale, made errors reading his own old drawings, and gave up a consultancy he had continued into retirement. Memory difficulty followed: he forgets conversations and cannot retain a message, and his wife says that reminding him of the context does not help. He has become mildly slower but she is emphatic that slowness is not the problem: the problem is that he 'cannot see how things fit together' and does not remember. There have been no abrupt events, no weakness, no speech disturbance and no gait change. He has hypertension of eighteen years, treated, and well-adhered CPAP for sleep apnoea. There is no family history of dementia. He declines any spinal procedure after a difficult lumbar fusion, and refuses a lumbar puncture when it is offered. There are no hallucinations, no fluctuation and no dream enactment.
